stories.title: Rust driver framework gains stable ABI for kernel modules
stories.text:
The Rust-for-Linux effort landed a stable kernel driver ABI this cycle, letting out-of-tree drivers compile against a fixed interface.

Maintainers report the first wave of ported drivers covers network cards and a scheduler-aware block layer. The kernel community debated versioning at length; the final scheme pins per-syscall surfaces and lets a driver declare the oldest kernel it supports.

stories.title: Scheduler patches land for mixed-criticality workloads
stories.text:
The EEVDF scheduler rework now exposes deadline classes that batch jobs cannot starve, and early numbers show p99 tail latency cut by a third.

Audio distributors report the change removes most of their xrun workarounds. The kernel scheduler maintainers caution that throughput-heavy benchmarks may regress slightly while the deadline logic settles.

stories.title: Coding agents adopt an open status protocol for terminals
stories.text:
A handful of terminal agents now report working, blocked, done or idle over an escape sequence, so the terminal emulator can route attention instead of the human polling tabs.

The protocol is deliberately tiny: one line, no network, no content. Window managers and multiplexers are the intended consumers.

stories.title: The quiet rise of small webservers
stories.text:
A survey of single-binary webservers that serve tens of thousands of requests per second from one process, no containers, no sidecars.

The author argues the industry default of layered infrastructure lost the plot: most applications need one binary, one config file, and a systemd unit.

stories.title: SQLite as an application file format, revisited
stories.text:
Ten years on, storing your document in a SQLite database instead of XML or JSON holds up well: transactions, incremental writes, and a query language for free.

The piece walks through schema patterns for hierarchical data and benchmark indexes for full-text search inside an application file.

stories.title: Ask HN: is anyone still using makefiles?
stories.text: A thread on build systems that circles, as always, back to make. Commenters defend the humble makefile for its debuggability and ubiquity, while others describe their migration to task runners and back again.

stories.title: Postgres query planner learns to love your covering indexes
stories.text:
New planner statistics make covering indexes picked more often, cutting heap access for wide tables.

The writeup includes a set of EXPLAIN ANALYZE before/afters on a 400GB database and a checklist for spotting index bloat the planner quietly ignores.

stories.title: A tmux config that survives four machines and ten years
stories.text:
Notes on keeping a terminal multiplexer setup portable: no plugins, one status line, ssh agent forwarding that works across hops.

The author's rule: every keybinding must be justifiable in a comment, or it goes.

stories.title: Small models, honest latency: running inference on the laptop
stories.text:
Benchmarks of 3B-parameter models on consumer laptops, with and without GPU offload, measuring time-to-first-token rather than throughput.

The surprising result: quantization matters less than prompt caching for interactive agent loops.

stories.title: Container queries changed how I write CSS layouts
stories.text:
A practical tour of container queries replacing a decade of resize observers and parent-scoped hacks.

Every example ships as a single HTML file, no build step, and the article argues the platform quietly outgrew most component frameworks' layout stories.

stories.title: Deleting code as a first-class engineering activity
stories.text:
A team made deletion a scheduled, celebrated task: every sprint ends with a rota for removing dead paths, unused flags and stale abstractions.

Six months in, onboarding time halved and the bug tracker thinned. The mechanics: a dead-code report in CI, and a rule that any deletion ships without a compensating abstraction.

stories.title: Tracing syscall latency with eBPF without drowning in data
stories.text:
A walkthrough of a 40-line eBPF program that histograms syscall latency per process, plus the kernel plumbing that makes it cheap enough to leave running in production.

Includes the flamegraphs that caught a regressions in a driver's error path.
